subject: Maximum likelihood and random effects; problem.

messages.author: b3204ecc9b0f3f36
messages.subject: Maximum likelihood and random effects; problem.
parts:
I am helping teach a course in hierarchical models, and want to show the students (a plurality of whom are grad students in education) how to use Stan from R. They've already learned how to use lme4, and so they're familiar with MLE procedures. I wanted to start by using Stan for MLE-like estimation, so they could treat the outcome as they're used to with an MLE. In other words, to use the "optimizing" command and invert the Hessian, rather than doing MCMC.

So, I went off and started to build some of the simple hierarchical models we've worked with, in Stan. And at first, it seemed to work; the estimates were close enough to the comparable ones from lmer, that I could chalk up any small differences to the effects of the priors I was using. (We're teaching them to use either minimally-informative priors like inv_gamma(.001,.001), for consistency with what they've done before; or, better, to use weakly-informative priors like T₃.)

But when the data set was a little bit smaller, there was sometimes a problem: Stan would want to set the variance of the random effects to zero. For a while, I couldn't figure it out. After all, wasn't this just MLE; and if there was a problem with Stan, shouldn't there be a similar problem with lmer?

Then I realized: lmer's MLE maximizes the likelihood conditional on the parameters, and only fits the random effects once it's done so; but Stan is effectively maximizing the likelihood conditional on the parameters and the random effects. So setting variance for the random effects arbitrarily close to 0 means arbitrarily high likelihood.

(Note: I know there's standard terminology for the almost-a-likelihood that I'm maximizing here, but I can't recall it at the moment. Can somebody tell me the right words?)

So, as I see it, here are my options for avoiding this problem (though some are probably impractical):
1. Just give up and use MCMC. The problem comes from using a Bayesian tool for frequentist procedures; the fix is to not do that. However, this means giving the students more theory and practical tricks than I want to; and it's also a lot slower than maximization.
2. Use variational methods (ADVI). Since these fit a seperable approximation of the full posterior, I can easily integrate out over the random effects, and find the maximum of the thing I want. Unfortunately, this is not yet possible with rstan.
3. Try to correct for this. Basically, if I could integrate over the random effects, that would be like subtracting the log of the precision with which I know them, which is proportional to the Fisher information conditional on both the data and the parameters which I'm maximizing but using expectation over the random effects. Assuming rough normality, the precision with which I know each random effect is basically a sum of the precision from the next level up — the inverse variance of the hyperdistribution — and the precision from the next level down — in the simplest case, the inverse variance of the residuals, divided by the number of observations in the relevant group. So, roughly speaking, I could adjust the log likelihood by adding log(sigma_alpha+sigma_y/harmonic_mean(n_j)), where each n_j is the size for group j.
4. Ignore the problem. Put a prior on the log of the random effect variance that's strong enough to keep it from slamming into zero, and live with the fact that it's downwardly biased and not as good as the number I'd get from lmer.

I'm leaning towards option 3, and being a bit fast and loose with the math (as you can already see from my suggestion of using harmonic means). But I'd like advice from the list. Is my understanding of the problem reasonable? Are the solutions I've enumerated better or worse than I think they are, in terms of either feasibility or effectiveness? Are there other ways to deal with this? What key words do I need to search for find the literature on this kind of issue?

Thanks a lot,
Jameson

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Maximum likelihood and random effects; problem.
parts: > (We're teaching them to use either minimally-informative priors like inv_gamma(.001,.001), for consistency with what they've done before; or, better, to use weakly-informative priors like T₃.)
Andrew is having a strong influence — I’m starting to get chills every time I see inv_gamma(.001,.001) priors...
> (Note: I know there's standard terminology for the almost-a-likelihood that I'm maximizing here, but I can't recall it at the moment. Can somebody tell me the right words?)

> 1. Just give up and use MCMC. The problem comes from using a Bayesian tool for frequentist procedures; the fix is to not do that. However, this means giving the students more theory and practical tricks than I want to; and it's also a lot slower than maximization.

Not really — optimization in Stan yields a perfectly fine frequentist ML estimator. It’s more that the asymptotics
necessary to motivate said estimator are not valid for hierarchical models.

> 2. Use variational methods (ADVI). Since these fit a seperable approximation of the full posterior, I can easily integrate out over the random effects, and find the maximum of the thing I want. Unfortunately, this is not yet possible with rstan.

This would give you something of a weird estimator — in particular I have no idea how you’d analyze its sampling
distribution.

> 3. Try to correct for this. Basically, if I could integrate over the random effects, that would be like subtracting the log of the precision with which I know them, which is proportional to the Fisher information conditional on both the data and the parameters which I'm maximizing but using expectation over the random effects. Assuming rough normality, the precision with which I know each random effect is basically a sum of the precision from the next level up — the inverse variance of the hyperdistribution — and the precision from the next level down — in the simplest case, the inverse variance of the residuals, divided by the number of observations in the relevant group. So, roughly speaking, I could adjust the log likelihood by adding log(sigma_alpha+sigma_y/harmonic_mean(n_j)), where each n_j is the size for group j.

Lots of assumptions in there which can lead to odd behaviors in the estimators. At the very least it will require
lots of empirical investigation to understand the ultimate performance.

> 4. Ignore the problem. Put a prior on the log of the random effect variance that's strong enough to keep it from slamming into zero, and live with the fact that it's downwardly biased and not as good as the number I'd get from lmer.
I believe this is the best option until you can (approximately or numerically) marginalize out the random effects.

>
> Andrew is having a strong influence — I’m starting to get chills every time I see inv_gamma(.001,.001) priors...

Check out the advice in our manual and in the papers of Andrew's
we've cited. Those inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001), contrary to popular belief,
have a huge impact on posteriors because of how they concentrate prior
mass.

>
>> (Note: I know there's standard terminology for the almost-a-likelihood that I'm maximizing here, but I can't recall it at the moment. Can somebody tell me the right words?)
>
> Maximum marginal likelihood.

AKA "empirical Bayes", but we also discourage that term because
it's no more empirical than full Bayes --- it's just a biased
approximation (the bias is underestimating lower level parameter
posterior variance and arises from treating the hierarchical parameters
as having a point estimate).
